Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they actually happen, not when money changes hands. For example, if you send an invoice in June but get paid in July, accrual shows the sale in June. If you receive a bill in June but pay it in July, accrual counts the cost in June. 

Cash-basis accounting does the opposite: it records income and expenses only when cash is received or paid. That makes cash-basis simple and easy to follow, but it can hide what your business really owes or is owed at any moment.

Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing business health because it shows money you’ll get and bills you still need to pay. That makes planning, comparing months, and understanding profitability more accurate. It’s a bit more work to keep up, but it’s better when you want a true view of how your business is performing.
